doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Coltrane, Powell and other jazz men playing R&B behind her
summary: Brown says Coltrane, Richard Powell and others played in R&B bands she toured with, and ties jazz to New Orleans funerals.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: You know I want to ask you a question here. As we can kind of try to relate this to jazz, you say the music was expensive because it cost you something. And I was thinking there seems to be a spiritual aspect, even to the jazz, even, but a lot of preachers said, oh, that’s the devil’s music. But at the same time many of those were the backup musicians for the R&B groups.

Of course. John Coltrane was in my band. We went through the south. John Coltrane was in my band, he was in Paul “Hucklebuck” Williams, who had the big record “The Hucklebuck” before Chubby Checker got it and called it “The Twist.” John Coltrane was in that band. I toured all through the south with Johnny Hodges, Richard oh, God he was killed in the car with Clifford Brown —

Richard Powell was my pianist. You see, Bud Powell’s brother. He was my pianist, you know? And I’m saying Kenny Burrell, all of them at one time or the other played that music, because that’s the basis of everything that they do. You know and if jazz indeed had its beginning in New Orleans, please, what was that, you know? The funerals? You’ve got to see that, have you ever seen one in New Orleans? You know what that’s like. If you can stay still, I’ll bet you, you can’t. But that’s like the old people used to say you rejoice at the going out and you weep at the coming in. And that’s what that music is about. But there is a very fine line. I always said that I would suppose that truly the difference between the real jazz musicians and the Gospel or rhythm & blues artists is that the technique, the improvisation, they had to know a little something about the written note, I would think. Because there were a few that I knew who had no knowledge of it. Wes Montgomery.
